title: Advent
hookLine: four weeks of waiting, a wreath of four candles, one lit each Sunday

cards: Early December. The stores have been playing Christmas music since before Halloween. Every screen says buy, hurry, celebrate now.
Then you walk into a Catholic church and it's quiet, and purple, and there's no Christmas tree yet. Just a ring of evergreen with four candles, and only one of them lit.
It can feel stubborn, like the Church missed the memo. It's on purpose. Before the feast, the Church asks for something the rest of December has almost forgotten how to do.

teach.b: Advent comes from the Latin adventus, a coming or an arrival. In the Roman world it was used for an emperor arriving to visit a city. Christians used it for the coming of Christ.

Advent begins four Sundays before Christmas, the first season of the Church year, and it looks two ways at once. The first part looks ahead to the end of time, when Christians believe Christ will come again.
The last part, especially from December seventeenth, looks back to his first coming, at Bethlehem.

teach.h: HE HAS COME, AND IS COMING.
teach.b: So Advent waits for someone who has come, and who is still coming. The Advent wreath is a later custom, and a lovely one.
A popular story traces it to Johann Wichern, a Lutheran pastor in Hamburg in the 1830s, who put candles on a cartwheel so the children in his orphanage could count down the days.
The idea spread, and Catholics took it up too.

teach.h: A WREATH: THREE VIOLET, ONE ROSE.
teach.b: Today it's usually a circle of evergreen with four candles, three violet and one rose, one more lit each Sunday.

The rose one is for the third Sunday, Gaudete, the rejoicing from yesterday. Advent is a season of preparing, penitential but not grim. The prophet Isaiah is read a lot, promising light to people in darkness.
People sing the old hymn O come, O come, Emmanuel, built on antiphons the Church prays in the last days before Christmas.
Families keep the wait in their own ways. Filipino Catholics have Simbang Gabi, nine Masses before dawn, starting December sixteenth.
In Mexico and across Latin America there's Las Posadas: nine nights of neighbors acting out Mary and Joseph knocking at doors, asking for room.
The whole season practices a skill December makes hard: waiting without rushing, and letting wanting grow.

how: In Advent, Catholic churches turn violet, and some families keep an Advent wreath at home, lighting one more of its four candles each Sunday, often with a short Scripture reading.

s: Advent is only about remembering Bethlehem
it also looks ahead to Christ's coming again, then back to his first coming.
the Advent wreath began among Lutherans
a popular story traces it to Johann Wichern in 1830s Hamburg; Catholics took it up later.
Advent is the first season of the Church year
the year begins on the first Sunday of Advent.

games.q: it's early December. the stores are all Christmas. your parish is violet and quiet. what is Advent asking of you?
o: wait, and prepare, before the feast.
games.why: Advent keeps the waiting: four weeks of preparing, so the feast arrives as a feast.

practice: If you have a candle and can light it safely, do; if not, picture one, and watch the flame. Think of something you're waiting for right now, news, a person, healing, a change, and let the waiting be quiet, not anxious.
If you pray, offer the waiting to God; if you don't, just keep the flame company.

wordCard.voice: Advent. From the Latin for an arrival. Four weeks of waiting before Christmas, one candle more each Sunday. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: an arrival or coming, once used for an emperor's visit to a city.

carryVoice: Your line: wait well. A long line can be a small Advent. See you tomorrow.
